summary:
Identity documents are the sharpest risk a trans visitor faces. Since January 2025 an executive order requires all identity documents issued by the national government to reflect sex assigned at birth. The passport agency stopped processing the "X" marker, available since 2022, and stopped issuing markers that do not match sex assigned at birth; existing "X" passports remain valid until expiration, while new and renewed applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents. The ACLU sued the foreign affairs department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports. Travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, leaving some trans and nonbinary citizens stranded abroad. Lambda Legal maintains guidance on what documentation to consider and how name and gender changes interact with national records under the changed policy.

Airport screening is invasive of privacy and can out trans travellers. The A4TE airport-security guide documents secondary screening, screening devices and pat-downs as the specific mechanisms, and sets out practical limits on prohibited items and carry-on quantities for trans passengers moving through checkpoints. A trans traveller was detained at the border for weeks and deported in January 2025, and a border officer faces a lawsuit over alleged sexual contact with a trans traveller at a major airport.

State document rules are tightening. Kansas enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not match sex assigned at birth and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities; the state now prevents trans people from changing markers on either document. Rights groups describe the Kansas law as a template other states may copy, and further targeting bills are pending in state legislatures.

Facility bans carry criminal exposure. State bathroom bans applying to trans people cover K-12 schools and some government buildings in 9 states and 1 territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states; 29 states, 4 territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. In some states trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances. In April 2025 a trans student was handcuffed in a women's restroom at a state capitol after declaring an intent to break the law; civil-rights attorneys describe it as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law.

Foreign governments now warn their own citizens about travelling here. Multiple countries issued advisories over identity-document and data rules in April 2025, and at least eight European states, among them Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country in March 2025, following detentions of European citizens over visa issues. Dated state-level travel-risk guidance issued in July 2026 flags 4 states as do-not-travel for trans people, with Idaho the most recently added.
tangentialFactors:
The document and facility rules sit inside a wider federal order programme. Executive Order 14168 establishes sex as a binary and addresses documents, a facilities clause and care funding; Order 14183 bans trans service members; Order 14187 concerns care for minors; Order 14190 addresses schools; Order 14201 addresses sports. A federal funding freeze followed in January 2025. Several of these orders have been blocked or enjoined in court.

Sport and entry rules extend to visitors. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, titled "Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports", was followed on 25 February 2025 by an announcement from the foreign affairs department banning trans athletes from entering the country to compete in women's sports; visa applicants are flagged with the code SWS25, and applicants listing a gender other than sex assigned at birth face a permanent ban on grounds of fraud.

Reporting from March 2026 places the conflict beyond sports and youth gender medicine, with policy and legal battles expanding into bathroom restrictions, health-care limits and document rules across states, Kansas among the battlegrounds. A travel guide published in April 2026 notes there is no national sodomy law, that safety varies by state, and advises checking recent violence reports before travel.

Equality-map data tracks state driver's licence, birth-certificate and name-change rules for trans people, setting out which states permit gender-marker changes and under what conditions.
localsOnly:
Residents of Kansas cannot obtain a birth certificate or driver's licence reflecting a gender marker other than sex assigned at birth, and are barred from sex-segregated facilities under the state's enacted law.

Residents in 9 states and 1 territory face bathroom bans in K-12 schools and some government buildings, with additional states imposing outright bans on facility use according to gender identity; in some states the conduct is a criminal offence in certain circumstances. Residents in 29 states, 4 territories and the District of Columbia live under no such ban.

State rules on driver's licences, birth certificates and name changes for trans residents differ, with policy tables setting out which states allow marker changes and the conditions attached.

Trans residents face the federal orders directly: the military ban under Order 14183, restrictions on care for minors under Order 14187, school provisions under Order 14190, sports provisions under Order 14201 and the January 2025 funding freeze. New and renewed passports issued to residents show sex assigned at birth regardless of gender identity or name change.
outOfScopeNotes:
The passport policy is challenged in federal courts and several of the executive orders have been blocked or enjoined; the current operative position of each is not settled by the sources here.

The ACLU action on behalf of seven plaintiffs and the lawsuit against the border officer are both described as pending, with no outcome stated.

Further targeting bills are pending in state legislatures and had not been enacted at the time of reporting.

The identity-document policy tables are undated, so the state-by-state conditions they record may not reflect the position at the time of travel.

The April 2026 travel guide instructs readers to check recent violence reports before travel; no such report data is included in this record.
